archetype.name: Bubble Team (special-teams-and-Saros)
archetype.definition: A Nashville side whose standings position is real for now but is built on an elite power play, an elite penalty kill and Juuse Saros rather than on winning the 5-on-5 game, which leaves it around the playoff line rather than comfortably above it.

report.headline: Special teams and Saros are covering for a team losing 5-on-5.
report.take:
Nashville sits third in the Central at 8-4-5 and on pace for 101 standings points, a jump from the 86 it posted last season and the 68 the year before. The goal ledger tells a calmer story. The Predators have scored 52 and allowed 51, a differential of 1 that ranks 15th in the league per game. They have banked 1.8 points beyond what that differential implies, fifth-most in the league, helped by a run of overtime games that broke their way late. This is a .500-by-margin team with a better-looking record.

The engine is everything except even strength. The power play converts 29.8% (4th) and the penalty kill holds at 88.5% (3rd), both far above league averages of 22.5% and 77%. Saros has been the other pillar: .912 with 6.5 goals saved above expected over 12 starts, nearly all of the team's 6.9 GSAx. Up front, Steven Stamkos (10 goals, 11 PP points), Filip Forsberg (20 points) and Ryan O'Reilly (17 points) drive the scoring, and Roman Josi's 20 points from 25.49 minutes a night make him the blueline's one real asset.

What the numbers hide is the 5-on-5 play. Nashville owns 47.8% of the expected goals (24th) and 45% of the shot attempts (28th), and it is out-shot 27.8 to 26.4 a game. Its 5-on-5 PDO is a neutral 99.9, so the even-strength results aren't being propped up by luck. They are simply mediocre. The all-situations PDO of 102.1 (9th) is where the inflation lives, and that comes from special teams and the goalie. The blueline grades a D. Past Josi, the regulars run from 101st to 191st on the defense tab, and Jayden Struble's 40.3% and Brady Skjei's 44% expected-goal shares show who is bleeding the chances Saros keeps erasing.

The last five games, 4-1-0 with 18 goals for and 12 against, show the formula working at full strength rather than a new team emerging. A penalty kill near 88% has no precedent in this franchise's recent history, which sits around 82%. The power play has run at about 22-23% in recent seasons. Both should drift back. When they do, Nashville will need either a Saros season for the ages or genuinely better 5-on-5 play to stay ahead of Colorado and Utah, who are right behind it.

strengths.title: Elite special teams on both sides
strengths.body: The power play at 29.8% and the penalty kill at 88.5% are both top-four in the league, and that gap over the league is the main reason a team losing at 5-on-5 has a positive goal differential. The power play is concentrated in Stamkos, Josi, O'Reilly and Forsberg, so it has real talent behind it. Both rates sit well above last season's 23.1% and 81.7%, though, so expect some give, especially on the kill.

strengths.title: Saros is stealing goals
strengths.body: Saros has saved 6.5 goals above expected and sits 7th on the goalie tab, the reason the defense ranks 6th in goals against despite allowing more shots than average. He has a track record of this kind of work; the franchise posted 61.5 GSAx in 2022-23. He is the most sustainable piece of the overachievement, but the gap behind him is steep: Justus Annunen is at .874.

strengths.title: A veteran top six that produces
strengths.body: Stamkos (10 goals), Forsberg (20 points) and O'Reilly (17 points) all rank inside the top 25 at their positions. Josi adds 20 points from the back end. Adam Edstrom (6 goals, 28th among centers) and Ross Colton give the bottom of the lineup some finish. Production this concentrated is real, but it leans heavily on power-play work.

concerns.title: Losing the 5-on-5 battle
concerns.body: An expected-goals share of 47.8% and a shot-attempt share of 45% put Nashville in the league's bottom third at even strength. Its 5-on-5 PDO of 99.9 means this isn't bad luck masking good play. Even the top line is under water: O'Reilly sits at 46.7% and Stamkos at 44.9%. This is the foundational problem, and nothing in the sheet suggests it is fixing itself.

concerns.title: A blueline that is Josi and little else
concerns.body: The defense grades a D. Skjei, Wilsby, Perbix, Hunt and Struble all rank 101st or worse on the defense tab, and Struble's 40.3% expected-goal share is the worst among the regulars. That group is why Saros faces more shots than the league average. It won't improve without personnel changes.

concerns.title: Record running ahead of the margin
concerns.body: A differential of 1 across 17 games doesn't usually produce a 101-point pace. Nashville's 1.8 points over its goal differential ranks 5th, a product of close and overtime results. That kind of edge rarely holds over a full season.

trend.note: After a choppy October, Nashville is 4-1-0 over its last five with a +1.2 goal differential a game, its best stretch of the year. It has been built mostly on goaltending and special teams rather than improved 5-on-5 play.

weekAhead.headline: Western road trip: three soft defenses and one real test
weekAhead.body:
All four games are on the road, starting with a back-to-back in Los Angeles and Anaheim. Three of the four opponents rank 17th or lower on the site, and each of those three allows more than expected to opposing forwards. The Kings (29th) have the league's worst penalty kill at 62.5% and bottom-five goaltending by GSAx. That is a natural target for a power play converting nearly 30%. San Jose (28th) ranks 30th in offense and 29th in defense, though its A- goaltending can keep games tighter than its record suggests.

The outlier is Vegas, 5th on the site with a 52.8% expected-goal share. The Golden Knights hold centers further under their averages than any team in the league, a direct problem for a Nashville attack that runs through Stamkos and O'Reilly. Anaheim is a strange matchup: 4th in offense on a league-best 38.5% power play and a 15.4% shooting rate, but 30th in defense with an .869 save percentage. The back-to-back raises the question of whether Annunen gets a start, which would remove Nashville's biggest edge for a night.

keyMatchups.title: Nashville power play vs. Kings kill
keyMatchups.body: Nashville's 29.8% power play meets a Los Angeles penalty kill that ranks last in the league at 62.5%. The Kings also allow the third-most points to centers relative to expectation, exactly where Stamkos and O'Reilly do their damage. This is the week's clearest edge.

keyMatchups.title: Ducks' power play vs. Nashville kill
keyMatchups.body: Anaheim's league-best 38.5% power play runs straight into Nashville's 3rd-ranked 88.5% kill. The Ducks' 15.4% shooting rate is the kind that fades, and their .869 save percentage gives Nashville's shooters a soft target. Staying out of the box limits Anaheim's only real weapon.

keyMatchups.title: Vegas smothers centers
keyMatchups.body: Vegas ranks 1st at holding centers under their expected output and 2nd against forwards overall. That puts Nashville's center-driven scoring up against its toughest possible opponent. Vegas also out-chances teams at 5-on-5, so this one likely rests on Saros and the power play.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Nashville can hold its own at 5-on-5 against Vegas, the one opponent this week that won't hand it special-teams or goaltending advantages.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect Nashville to cool from its 101-point pace. The penalty kill and power play are running well above the team's recent norms, and an edge of nearly two points over the goal differential is the kind that evens out. What should last is Saros, who gives the Predators a real chance to win most nights, and a top six with enough finish to keep the power play dangerous even as it regresses. What drags the outlook down is a 5-on-5 game in the league's bottom third and a blueline graded D.

The realistic landing spot is the playoff bubble: somewhere around 87 to 97 standings points and 37 to 42 wins. That means fighting Colorado and Utah for Central position, with a wild card as the likeliest route in. A Saros injury or slump would push the projection to the bottom of that range quickly given Annunen's start. A real improvement in shot share would be the only thing that makes the top of the range comfortable.
swingFactors: How far the special teams regress
Whether the third pair stops bleeding 5-on-5 chances

confidence.note: 17 games is enough to trust the shot-share story, but special-teams and goaltending rates are still volatile.
